title: Boardroom crisis: 1-minute demo
headline: The first six hours, in one minute
subtitle: A breach is under way. Three quick calls, then see what each choice costs.

briefing.text: Do take your time... I have all day. You have until 14:00.

fallout.text: Ah, the ledger. Let's see what you cost yourselves...

briefing.turtle_intro: Welcome to the room, dear. It is 08:10 and the board is waiting. Three calls, one minute.

timeline.text: The security tool flags 40 GB leaving a file server for an unknown address. The alert waits in a queue.
**Now.** The board is called into the crisis room, and you take the chair.

known: Files on several servers are encrypted, and it is still spreading.
A large upload left the network at 07:40.
unknown: How they got in, and whether they are still inside.
Whether customer data was copied, and whose.
briefing.spider_line: Six hours. Plenty of time to make mistakes... I do hope you make some.
briefing.note_title: A little note for the board
note: Pay me €1.2 million in crypto before 14:00 and I will send the key. Refuse, and at 14:00 the copy goes online and the key is destroyed.

playbook.intro: Two rules cover the first hours. Tap a card to read it up close.

cards.title: Contain, then think
cards.say: A panicking board makes the attacker's job easy. Do the boring things first, in the right order, and keep the evidence.

rules.headline: Cut the cable, keep the power.
rules.body: Disconnect affected machines from the network, but don't switch them off or wipe them. The evidence lives in memory and on disk.

rules.headline: Say only what you can prove.
rules.body: "No data was affected" is a promise. Break it once and nobody believes your next update.

cards.sign_off: Calm isn't a feeling. It's an order of operations.

cards.title: Nobody does this alone
cards.say: I have seen many storms, dear. The boards that came through them well were never the cleverest. They simply called the right people early and told the truth.

rules.headline: Call the experts before you decide anything big.
rules.body: Legal, your insurer, the police and an incident response team come first. That includes the ransom: paying guarantees nothing and funds the next attack.

rules.headline: Tell the right people, on time.
rules.body: A regulator's clock starts when you become aware: 72 hours under GDPR, "as soon as possible" in Switzerland. Customers need clear steps before the attacker leaks the data.

cards.sign_off: A team that stays calm in the storm was looked after long before it.

cat0.label: Cat's first rule: cut the cable

cat2.label: Cat's second rule: say only what you can prove

turtle0.label: Turtle's first rule: call the experts

turtle1.label: Turtle's second rule: tell the right people

decisions_intro.text: Three decisions. Lock each one in and I'll check it. No takebacks. Watch the four dials.

decisions.title: Stop the spread
decisions.text: The encryption is moving from server to server. Dana is on the line and needs an order right now. What do you tell her?

artifact.name: Dana Keller
artifact.text: It's spreading. Fourteen servers in ten minutes, and the backup server is next on its list. Tell me what to do, Sam.

options.text: Cut the affected machines off from the network, but leave them switched on. Nobody wipes anything.
Switch everything off and wipe it, then rebuild from scratch. A clean slate.
options.why: You wiped the evidence along with the problem. Now nobody can show which door I used or what I took, so you must assume I took everything... and I still have the key to that door.

options.text: Wait until IT has the full picture, then act in one go.
options.why: While the board waited for a full picture, I finished the painting. By 09:00 the backup server was locked too, and your best way out had gone.

options.text: Tell every employee to reboot their computer, which usually clears this sort of thing.
options.why: Rebooting wiped the traces held in memory, the ones investigators wanted most. And my encryption simply woke up again with each machine.

decisions.explain: Isolate first, ask questions later. Pulling the network cable stops the spread, and leaving the power on keeps the evidence in memory and on disk. Investigators need it to find the way in and to learn what was copied.
decisions.spider_ok: Hm. A cable pulled and the evidence untouched. I had nine more servers on my list... and now no way to reach them.
decisions.best: Disconnect the affected machines from the network, leave them powered on, and wipe nothing.

decisions.title: The ransom
decisions.text: The note demands €1.2 million in crypto before 14:00. After that the stolen copy goes online and the key is destroyed. Where does the board stand?

artifact.name: Dana Keller
artifact.text: Last night's backup sits on the same network, so I can't promise it's clean. The board needs a position on the note before the press finds it.

options.text: Don't pay yet. Call the police, and let legal and the response team check the backups and the options first.
Pay now, before the clock runs down. It's the fastest way to get the files back.
options.why: Thank you for the money... My key opened a third of your files. I kept my copy of your data, naturally. And now I know that this board pays.

options.text: Reply from the CEO's mailbox and haggle the price down yourselves.
options.why: How brave... You wrote like frightened amateurs, and I am no amateur. Each reply told me how badly you needed those files, so each reply raised the price.

options.text: Refuse, and tell nobody outside this room. Fewer people knowing means fewer leaks.
options.short: Telling no one outside the room
options.why: Silence. My favourite. No police, no one who has met me before... You made yourselves quite alone.

decisions.explain: Paying is never a reflex. It buys no promise of a working key, no promise the stolen copy is deleted, and it funds the next attack. Call the police, bring in legal and the responders, test what your backups can really restore, and decide on facts, not on a countdown.
decisions.spider_ok: No payment. No panic. I do hate a patient board.
decisions.best: Don't pay yet. Involve the police, legal and the responders, and test the backups first.

decisions.title: Customers and the regulator
decisions.text: The responders confirm it: about 40 GB were copied, including the names, emails and hashed passwords of 120,000 customers. The attacker says it goes public at 14:00. What do you do about the regulator and your customers?

artifact.name: Luc Marchand
artifact.text: Under GDPR the clock to tell the authority is 72 hours from when we became aware. Swiss law says as soon as possible. Our clock started at 07:40, whatever we decide.

options.text: Notify the data protection authority now, and prepare a plain message for customers: what happened, what was taken, and what to do.
Wait until the investigation is finished, then decide who to tell.
options.why: An investigation takes weeks. The legal deadline takes three days. The regulator will ask why you knew on Friday and spoke on Tuesday... and fines are written in percentages.

options.text: Say nothing unless the data actually appears online.
options.why: At 14:00 I published. Your customers learnt it from a stranger on a forum, with no warning and no chance to change a password. Several accounts fell by evening.

options.text: Email every customer now: 'your data is safe'. Investigate afterwards.
options.why: 'Your data is safe.' Such a lovely sentence to send an hour before I proved it false. Trust takes years to build, and one sentence to spend.

decisions.explain: Be early, be plain, be true, dear. The regulator's clock started when you became aware, and customers need to change passwords and watch for phishing before the attacker gets to them. Never promise safety you can't prove.
decisions.spider_ok: You told them yourselves, and plainly. That leaves me nothing to threaten with.
decisions.best: Tell the regulator on time, and tell customers plainly what happened and what to do.

contained.title: Hm. You closed every door I tried.
contained.body: Isolated, informed, patient, honest and kind. I did not enjoy that at all. I'll look for a house with a quieter board... and fewer second factors.
contained.score: Three out of three, dear. Notice that none of it needed a clever tool, only the right order. Now go and ask your own team whether the VPN has a second lock.

bruised.title: You're still standing... but I left marks.
bruised.body: Most of it, you handled. A few of your choices were gifts, and I kept them. The ledger below shows exactly which.
bruised.score: Mostly sound. The ones that went wrong are in the recap, each with the rule that would have saved you. Read them, then replay.

wrecked.title: What a lovely mess we made together.
wrecked.body: Every one of those choices felt reasonable at the time. That is exactly why they work on people. Try again, and this time, think about the order.
wrecked.score: That was a hard morning, dear, and it was meant to be. Real boards get these wrong too, which is why we practise. Read the recap, then try again.

footer: Until next time... the next note won't come by email. Do ask whether your VPN has a second lock.
